title: The Napoleon Jacket Is Making A Comeback This Fall—Here’s How To Style It & Our Favorites To Shop
text:
The Napoleon Jacket Is Making A Comeback This Fall—Here’s How To Style It & Our Favorites To Shop

Throwing on a bold layering piece is, often, all it takes to make a good outfit great and the timely resurgence of the Napoleon jacket — complete with epaulettes and columns of oversized buttons — among popular trends for 2026 just confirms it.

Despite the summer season still underway, I can’t help but notice the faint chill in the air when the sun goes down, which means colder weather is right around the corner and it’s time to start thinking about fall and winter wardrobes. If you’re like me, and prefer to keep your daily uniform easy yet elevated (think, some iteration of denim and a plain tee), then introducing something a little more festive into the mix as the temperature drops can make all the difference, especially when you want a little more flair. 

Of course, the military jacket is nothing new and has been through its fair share of trend cycles, coming out on the other end more powerful than before. Named after 19th-century French military leader Napoleon Bonaparte, the cropped uniform silhouette has since been adopted by the style set, with Yves Saint Laurent leading the way in the late 1960s. By the ’90s, Jean Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler were among some of the big names to put their own spin on the look.

Cultural icons like Michael Jackson and supermodel Kate Moss also began to embrace the trend, with the former making it an integral part of his stage presence. This only further cemented the jacket’s status within the fashion industry. Today, it’s defined by a strongly defined shoulder, navy, gold, white, and red color combos, and, of course, round embossed buttons (functional or not). 



Aside from the likes of Alexander McQueen and Ann Demeulemeester, who have been designing Napoleon jackets for decades, the last few seasons have seen a noticeable influx of brands, big and small, who are influenced by military uniforms. According to fashion psychologist Shakaila Forbes-Bell, this is always a sign of the times, as well as the industry’s current obsession with the indie sleaze aesthetic. “People like to use their style as a way to reflect the current cultural zeitgeist,” she previously told Refinery29. “[Shoppers are] dressing in styles that are a bit more utilitarian and pragmatic.” 

Back in February, I sat front row as Cinq à Sept debuted a fitted denim Napoleon jacket, paired with a pussy-bow blouse on its Fall 2026 runway in NYC. While later in the season, R13 offered a super wearable take on the trend in longline and oversized silhouettes emblazoned with the same large, round buttons you’d expect on more traditional styles. Meanwhile, cool-girl brand EB Denim’s “Ford” Jacket feels like a more posh, updated version that has the same versatility as a classic black blazer. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Style The Napoleon Jacket

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Shelby Ying Hyde (@theshelbyying)

When it comes to embracing the look IRL, the key is to keep it super simple and straightforward, slipping it over generally unfussy ensembles to let the military-inspired details do all of the talking. I paired the vintage, Ralph Lauren version that I found on Poshmark with dark-wash flared jeans and a Tabi ballet flat for a family dinner, like it was 2006. 

Dua Lipa tends to take a more casual approach, wearing bright red and navy cropped styles by Ann Demeulemeester with denim and white T-shirts. Blackpink’s Jennie wore a custom Napoleon jacket by the brand for Lollapalooza in August, opting for a leather triangle bikini top underneath. Whereas, Brother Vellies creative director and founder of the 15 Percent Pledge, Aurora James took a more playful approach, styling her navy blue Napoleon-inspired Chanel Spring 2009 jacket with bloomer pants and mules—before ultimately slipping it over the classic white tee and denim combo, to show the secondhand style’s range. 

Whether you opt for an affordable Napoleon jacket for everyday wear or are looking to invest in a luxury piece for your personal archive, there are a bunch of different styles available on the market to choose from, many of which will make even the simplest of ensembles that much more interesting. The endless styling options are just the icing on the proverbial cake.

title: Anthropologie’s Beauty Advent Calendars Always Sell Out—And They’re Already Here
text:
Anthropologie’s Beauty Advent Calendars Always Sell Out—And They’re Already Here

It may not feel like it just yet, but there are some telltale signs that fall, let alone the holidays, are indeed right around the corner. It’s not just pumpkin spice lattes that are back earlier than ever: Believe it or not, holiday collections are already beginning to trickle into stores, including advent calendars.

These aren’t just any blockbuster beauty box sets; advent calendars make the countdown to Christmas the most glam 24 (or, in some cases, 12) days of the year. And there’s one to watch that sells out without fail: Anthropologie.

In recent years, the reader-favorite destination for fashion, home décor, and more has seriously amped up its beauty selection, stocking viral fragrance brands like DedCool and Phlur alongside body-care faves from Salt & Stone, Vacation, and many others. And since 2018, the retailer has compiled some of its bestselling brands into an annual advent calendar — aka a jam-packed value set that’s perfect for gifting, including to yourself.

The 24 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar, $98

And pretty much all of them can be found in the brand’s 24 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar. Retailing for $98 (but with a value of $301), this collection includes full-size and mini goodies from L’Occitane, Caudalie, Boy Smells, Stila, and more, all tucked inside a keepsake box featuring artwork by British-Filipina artist Nephthus Foster, whom Anthropologie has partnered with for the past three years on its holiday designs.

The 12 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar, $50

Looking for a more budget-friendly (but every bit as fun) unboxing experience? There’s also the 12 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar. title: Why Adults Is The Buzziest Show On TV, According To Star Lucy Freyer
text:
Why Adults Is The Buzziest Show On TV, According To Star Lucy Freyer

FX’s Adults is one of the buzziest new shows around. It’s a show that embraces the realities of life as a Gen-Zer in this chaotic world, and although it’s a laugh-out-loud comedy, it doesn’t shy away from real-world topics. In Season 1, there was an episode devoted to the cost of healthcare in the US, and the cliffhanger saw Paul Baker (Jack Innanen) struggle to immigrate as a Canadian citizen. Season 2 examines even more real-world issues, including language use, fear of aging as women, and our digital footprint. Lucy Freyer, the Australian star who plays Billie Schaeffer, tells Refinery29 that this could be why Adults resonates with so many viewers. Season 2 spoilers follow.

In Season 1, Issa Damani (Amita Rao) takes in a young teenager, Annabelle, who needs an abortion. Due to reproductive laws, she’s had to travel to New York to receive healthcare. The episode escalates, with Annabelle portrayed as an unlikeable, whiny character — but the point is clear. Everybody should have the right to reproductive healthcare, even if they’re annoying. “All of these ideas are packaged in this way that is sort of fun and easy. But when you think about it, you’re like, oh. [There’s] actually a lot to think about,” Freyer laughs.

In Season 2, Episode 7 “C Alert”, Anton Evans (Owen Thiele) gets in trouble when dropping the word “cunt” (complimentary) in a corporate setting. Many people from the LGBQTIA+ communities have taken back this word and use it in a positive way — see PEDESTRIAN.TV’s “cunty” moment with Pedro Pascal here — but it becomes a whole thing with the older, predominantly white NYC executives.

“When we read it, I was like, ‘Oh, it’s so brilliant!’,” Freyer recalls. “It’s about the evolution of language. David Foster Wallace has this essay that he wrote, which is actually a book review of a dictionary called Authority in American Usage and it’s about language.” She goes on to say that some people allow language to evolve, while others hold on to an idea of the traditional use of language. It’s these types of storylines that make us think deeper and keep us hooked.

One of Billie’s biggest hurdles this season is ageing. It sounds laughable, since her character is only 25, but it’s so easy to feel like you’re fighting an invisible clock. Again, it’s relatable. Freyer says she turned 30 while she was filming that particular episode, and was faced with an actor who played a younger version of her. “She’s so lovely and young, and [I thought], this could spin me out. But you know what? I’m exactly where I need to be, this is great,” Freyer says. “I think now ageing, especially for women, everything is happening later. It doesn’t matter. You don’t have any specific timeline… it used to be this idea of life ends when you turn 30, but [now] it’s like life feels like it’s just beginning, and in a big way.”

Part of the reason Freyer thinks the “ticking clock” conversation isn’t as relevant now is due to health technology advances like egg freezing and IVF — another big storyline in Adults Season 2. “Specifically for women who want to have [biological] children, there is that biological clock that sort of starts to play into the way you think about your existence after you turn 30,” the actor says. “I think now with egg freezing, it’s opened up a world for women to be like, actually, you know what? I’m going to throw those things on ice and live my life the way I want to live it, and not [have it] dictated by that timeline.”

The other big drawcard for Adults is that friendship sits at the heart of every episode. Friends are your chosen family, and seeing what Billie and the gang get up to in each episode can either give you nostalgia for earlier days or something to look forward to. “To be able to live with friends when things sort of don’t matter that much is the greatest joy you can possibly have in life,” Freyer declares. “Especially friendship when proximity is easy.”

The actor notes that when you get older, it becomes harder to have regular, quality time with your friends, even just because of location and schedules. But the sweet spot for Adults is the setting: when you still have housemates and can be so entrenched in each other’s lives. “When you’re living with your friends, and you don’t have things on in your life that matter that much, friendships can be the centre of your life,” she says.

“Issa and Billie’s relationship in this season, the way they explore it and how we end up sharing a room… I think that it’s such a beautiful depiction of friendship in your 20s.”

Adults Season 2 is now available to stream on FX.

title: Gabriella Karefa-Johnson On Owning Her Space, Hidden London Gems & The Rules Of Plane Perfume
text:
Gabriella Karefa-Johnson On Owning Her Space, Hidden London Gems & The Rules Of Plane Perfume

Besides a pilot, you’d be hard-pressed to find someone as well-traveled as Gabriella Karefa-Johnson. From the winding streets of London and the cobblestones of Paris to the glittering sands of Jamaica, the New York-based fashion editor and stylist — who made history as the first Black woman to style the cover of Vogue — has amassed a lifetime of memories, experiences, and, naturally, scents from the destinations that have shaped her work. Getting there, however, hasn’t always been smooth sailing — or flying.

“It’s difficult to exist sometimes in marginalized bodies,” says Karefa-Johnson, “so when you’re in this kind of like, rarefied air — as some might call first class — it can feel alienating, like there are eyes on you, like you’re not supposed to be there.” One thing she’ll never do? Shrink. “Or camouflage,” says Karefa-Johnson. “I’m going to be me wherever I am, and I think that that’s why I feel so comfortable in these places, because I bring myself authentically.”

London — in particular the eclectic melting pot that is Brixton — is one such place where she can truly be herself, with the surrounding scents creating memories that linger long after the vacation ends. But beyond the powdery, soapy blend of cashmeran, musk, and patchouli that makes the iconic Rosewood Hotel’s pillow mist so unforgettable, it’s the city’s everyday food smells that stay with her most: “Think fish and chips all wrapped in a newspaper, so you have that paper smell,” says Karefa-Johnson.

Ultimately, though, nowhere smells as good as home. “I want to be smelling like — honestly and truthfully — my mom,” says Karefa-Johnson. “I haven’t seen my mom in a really long time [but] I want to go back home to hug her more. I want to be around her enough for her brilliance to rub off on me. And I want to prioritize being with my family that is all in LA; I miss them dearly.” So what does that feeling of comfort smell like? EOS Vanilla Cashmere 24H Moisture Body Lotion, Body Wash, and Body Mist, of course.

Listen to the full podcast episode, where Karefa-Johnson joins Nose Dive host Asia Grant — an NYC-based independent perfumer and creative director — for a conversation about taking up space and being unapologetically herself, the best-smelling London hotspots, and the scents she’d avoid wearing on a plane.
